newsitem.title: UK: De Charette outlines French vision of NATO, EU.
newsitem.headline: De Charette outlines French vision of NATO, EU.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette called for a shared European command of NATO with the United States and emphasised the importance of an independent European Central Bank.

In an interview in the Financial Times, published on Thursday, de Charette outlined his vision for the military alliance and the European Union and insisted that the Franco-German plan for greater flexibility in the EU, allowing some members to pursue closer integration without waiting for the others, was not aimed at excluding Britain or any other member state.
He said France's request that a European be given command of NATO forces in the Mediterranean was as a "proposition, not a demand."
"We're not asking for anything," he said. "If we succeed, I don't see the French staging a celebration on the Champs Elysees. Any more than, if we fail, they are going to march on the Bastille."

Softening France's stance on the alliance which it is proposing to rejoin fully, he said NATO commands should be shared with the United States having overall strategic command of Europe and the Atlantic but Europeans having regional controls.
"We work on the assumption that Europe has, step by step, to build its own identity, to organise its own space, to establish its own currency, and fix its destiny."
He insisted there was no fundamental divergence between U.S. and European interests but warned, "no one can leave their vital interests to be defended by someone else -- not even an intimate friend."
De Charette denied that France was trying to undermine the independence of a planned European Central Bank, which was suggested by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer in remarks over the weekend.
"No one questions the European Central Bank's independence, and certainly not France. It's written in black and white in the Maastricht treaty. There is no debate on this point.
He explained that plans for greater flexibility and new forms of co-operation must be open to any EU member that subsequently wants to join.
"I think more of those who cannot than those who don't want to," he said, adding that he envisaged an enlarged EU with closer to 30 than 20 members.

Some countries will not be ready for new forms of integration as soon as others, he explained. De Charette also insisted that new flexibity within the EU framework would be in the interest of non members and the single market.
